title: Nothing before the work of God (ch. 43)
word: Nothing before the work of God
hook: when the bell rings, leave everything and go

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Office: the psalm says seven times a day, and Benedict made it a schedule. Your line was seven times a day. Did your three anchors hold? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

A monk is in the garden with a hoe, halfway down a row of beans. Another is in the library, one page from the end of a chapter. A third has his arms in a sink of hot water. Then the bell rings. Not a polite reminder on a phone that can be snoozed. The bell. Saint Benedict's Rule says what happens next: each of them sets down whatever is in his hands, right then, and goes. The beans can wait. The chapter can wait. The dishes can definitely wait. Today, chapter forty-three, and a short Latin line that runs the whole house: nothing before the work of God.
screen: `A HOE, A BOOK, A SINK.` → `THEN THE BELL.` → `PUT IT DOWN AND GO.`

segments.voice: Benedict's word for the hours of prayer is the work of God. Some readers hear in it more than the monks' work for God: God's work, which they join. Chapter forty-three says that at the hour of the Office, as soon as the signal is heard, the monks are to leave whatever they're doing and hurry. And then a small, careful brake: hurry, but with seriousness, so that nobody turns the dash to chapel into a joke. Then comes the line: let nothing be put before the work of God. Chapter five had a monk leave his work for a word from the abbot. Here it's a bell, and the reason is prayer itself. It's a claim about what a day is for. The garden matters, the books matter, the dishes matter. They just don't come first. What makes the chapter lovely is how human the rest of it is. Benedict knows some monks will be late. So for the night office, he asks that the opening psalm be said slowly, drawn out, to give latecomers time to arrive. Someone who comes in after it ends doesn't stay outside, either. Benedict worries that a monk left outside might go back to sleep, or sit by the door chatting. So the latecomer comes in and stands in a separate place, a little embarrassed, but inside. The bar is high, and the door stays open. For people who don't hear a monastery bell, the question is the same one. When something is ringing for prayer, what gets set down, and what makes it wait?
screen: `THE HOURS ARE THE WORK OF GOD.` · `AT THE SIGNAL, LEAVE IT AND HURRY.` · `THE PSALM GOES SLOWLY FOR LATECOMERS.` · `LATE, BUT INSIDE.` · then, large: `LET NOTHING BE PUT BEFORE THE WORK OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop mid-task to pray, and rehearse it now. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind start on something, anything: planning dinner, a list for tomorrow, a message you need to send. Get halfway into it. Then stop. Don't finish the thought. Set it down the way a monk sets down a hoe, and turn toward God, or simply toward the quiet, for a few breaths. Then let the thought come back if it wants to. Notice how hard it is to leave a thing unfinished. Later today, pick one moment to do this for real. If you pray, you can use any short prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Nothing before the work of God. Benedict's rule for the bell: when it's time to pray, everything else waits. Today's word.
screen: `NOTHING BEFORE THE WORK OF GOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nothing before prayer. Today, choose one time to stop in the middle, not at a tidy break, and pray or breathe before you finish. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries a bell calls the community to the hours, and monks and nuns leave their work to gather in choir; some Catholics outside monasteries pause at set times, such as the Angelus at noon.

pairs: Benedict's name for the hours of prayer

myth: Benedict tells monks to run to chapel as fast as they can, any way they can
hurry, he says, but with seriousness, so it never turns into a joke.
the night office's opening psalm is drawn out so latecomers can arrive
Benedict asks for it to be said slowly for that reason.
in the Rule, a late monk must wait outside the chapel

fork.setup: you're a monk who overslept. the night office has already begun when you reach the chapel door. what does the Rule ask?
options: stay outside so you don't disturb anyone.
come in and stand in a separate place.
go back to bed and come to the next hour.
fork.reveal: Benedict wants latecomers inside, standing apart, rather than outside, where they might sleep or chat.

original.note: Latin, the line from chapter forty-three: let nothing be put before the work of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: put prayer first means pray when the important stuff is done.
what it means: when the bell rings, the important stuff waits. prayer goes first.
what a scholar hears: Benedict calls the Office the opus Dei, the work of God, and pairs a strict rule with gentle provisions for latecomers.

notes: Editor pass: swapped the hook's pen-at-a-desk image (a monk at his pen had just appeared in day 1192 and day 1184) for a monk in the library; marked the 'God's work, which they join' gloss as some readers' reading rather than the narrator's.

The Rule is paraphrased; no translation of the Rule is on the public-domain list. Check the summary of ch. 43: leave whatever is in hand at the signal and hasten, yet with gravity so as not to give occasion for levity; 'Operi Dei nihil praeponatur'; the invitatory psalm (Psalm 94, Vulgate) said slowly at Vigils so latecomers can arrive; latecomers stand in the last place or a separate place, inside rather than outside, lest they sleep or gossip.
'Not the monks' work for God, exactly: God's work, which they join' is an interpretive gloss on 'opus Dei'; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
